en: Preface to the Carving of the Jewel Grotto of the Śrīmālā-sūtra Now,
that which is called the Great Vehicle of the One Vehicle is the precious carriage of the Dharma King. Therefore,
it is adorned with the rare treasures of myriad virtues to enhance its height and breadth, and equipped with the bells and chimes of the four analytical knowledges.
Hanging in rows along its sides, the balustrades hold it fast; with canopies and parasols cast aside in compassion, meditation-cords serve as mats and the pillow of tranquility provides rest.
Flower tassels dangle down, bringing joy to those from the four quarters who raise their feet to take refuge and look up in devotion;
with jeweled cords intertwined and draped, how could the multitudes have any fault of attachment or biased views?

When hosting guests, the offerings were abundant and reverent; when slaughtering oxen, the cuts were precise and skillful. How much more so for one whose household is wealthy and prosperous, who does not restrict their giving;
or one whose resources are never exhausted, who does not limit their calculations.
How magnificent! How sublime! Yet, the common masses wear folly like a crown and bind themselves with ignorance like a sash;

they constantly dance within the abode of sensory pleasures and flavors, yoked to the carriage of doubt and driven by delusion as they gallop toward the source of birth and death. They greedily crave fame and glory, finding peace in the midst of burning flames; they are stuck to their worldly existence like a bird to a sticky resin, never realizing they are like straw drifting on a river or dry reeds caught in a fire. Since they do not even perceive the pit of fire, how could they have leisure to discuss the precious chariot?

Thus, our Dharma King personally held up four alms bowls, and the teaching at the Deer Park was founded; until his body lay down between the twin śāla trees, the instruction through parables reached its ultimate conclusion.

Whenever the sound of the phoenix arises or the brilliance of gold shifts its luster, it is none other than out of compassion for those who are deaf and stubborn, and sorrow for those who are blind and ignorant.

Thus, the eminent figures such as Miaojixiang and Bianji assist their transformation, while the great heroes of the West and East support their governance. Therefore, whether through kindness or enmity, all serve to benefit sentient beings; whether met with praise or reproach, it is entirely the exercise of skillful means. The ultimate aim is solely to cause them to cast off the cap of delusion, untie the jade pendants of worldly entanglement, mount the great carriage, and drive along the broad thoroughfare.
There is here the Lady Śrīmālā, who occupies the position of consort in the inner palace; as for her original ground, who could possibly fathom it?
Her nature is gentle and virtuous, and her compassion is surely destined to be extraordinary.

On the morning when the message of the arrival at Vaiśālī was delivered, and on the day the image appeared in the void, he relied upon conditions to give rise to the teaching and entrusted matters to accord with the capacity of beings. When external demons of "fox-like" courage suddenly disrupted the proclamation of the refined rites, his lion’s roar of definitive meaning and his fearless lotus-eyes shone forth; he was truly like one of the loyal ministers of the Zhou dynasty—could he not be considered a giant among those who served as the spiritual influence of Jetavana?
The title of this sutra is *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-mahāvaipulya*.
Now, as for the "lion's roar," it is a definitive proclamation; were it not for the ultimate exhaustion of its principles, who could attain such certainty in its teaching?
The One Vehicle refers to the single Buddha-vehicle, which is the reality;
the Great Expedient Means refers to the teaching of various [vehicles], which is called skillful artifice.
Indeed, to ride without a vehicle and yet ride, with nothing upon which to ride—this is called the One Vehicle.
To move without movement and yet move, with nothing upon which to move—this is true movement.
Precisely because there is nothing it sets in motion, there is nothing it does not set in motion;
precisely because there is nothing it rides upon, there is nothing it does not ride upon.
If this is not so, by what name could one call that which is pointed out as such wondrous and profound mystery—the Great Vaipulya?
Yet the ultimate truth is profound and abstruse; though one reveres it, it is difficult to enter, leading to boundless sighs and lamentations.
The translated language is ancient and concise; readers fail to progress within it, often expressing regret and sorrow.

In the early Tang dynasty, there was the Great Master Zang of Jixiang, whose noble lineage originated from distant lands and whose refined character was born in harmony with the rivers and mountains; he inherited the fragrant legacy of Nāgārjuna and explored the secret tenets of Vulture Peak.

In the sharpness of debate, he vied with Kātyāyanīputra for brilliance; his eloquence surpassed that of autumn cicadas. As a treasury of wisdom, he rivaled Śāriputra in his store of knowledge; his elegance was like that of spring birds. He was truly a guiding master after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and an eminent model for the Dharma-gate.

Thereupon, he sighed that the subtle words had already been severed and lamented that the declining customs were not being revitalized. He spoke with bold resolve and engaged in profound discourse, distinguishing the true from the false within the principles of the teachings; his intentions and utterances clarified the ultimate destination, like the distinction between the Jing and Wei rivers.

Thus, he composed several volumes of commentaries to manifest this authentic exposition with penetrating clarity, and produced over one hundred thousand words to illuminate these profound mysteries with radiant brilliance.

Those who have not yet discussed its profundity but have already opened the golden treasury, and those who have translated it and truly peered into the treasure cave—are they not like those who, startled and intoxicated with madness, point out and show others the precious carriage?

Now, the request that these [texts] circulate within our realm has indeed crossed over waves ten thousand fathoms deep, and their transmission to this day has likewise passed through more than a millennium of frost and dew. While the land of China has already returned to the state of non-existence, the region of mulberry trees (China) has never fallen into the hands of the fire-god Huilu (destruction). Nevertheless, though the manuscripts have been preserved in secret, they have not moistened the parched throats of scholars;
and though the precious treasuries of the monasteries exist, how can they satisfy the yearning necks of those who admire antiquity?
Moreover, as constant dampness and humidity are ever to be feared, how could one prevent the damage of bookworms?

Here, I, [Name], have long venerated this scripture, hoping my mind might become profound and serene; having now obtained this commentary, I feel as if the thick ice within my heart has suddenly melted away.
Now, since it is said that whether one dwells in a village or a field, why should one abandon a bookstore?
And as we have heard that whether it be trees or stones, how could one discriminate between jujubes and pears?

Thus, disregarding my own lack of measure, I have ventured to propagate this work; though I have repeatedly collated and corrected it, I still fear the lingering dust of errors such as confusing "ru" for "lu."
I have again commissioned the engravers, rejoicing that the precious work has been spared from the ravages of water and dust.
My hope is that all men and women who encounter this shall together forge karmic bonds for future lives,
and that the benevolent and the wise shall be gathered in to ride together upon the Single Vehicle.
Thus it is said.
Written on an auspicious day in the final month of winter in the sixteenth year of the Genroku era, by the śramaṇa Dōkū, with humble greetings.
